messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 32
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

For the first three days of his captivity, Elias had been certain he was going to die. He had been working a remote trail in the Sierra Nevada when two men took him at gunpoint, driven him hours into the desert, and held him in an abandoned mining shack. They wanted information about a stash of stolen artifacts he had inadvertently stumbled upon, information he did not have. They did not believe him. Over the course of what he later learned was seventy-two hours, they burned the soles of his feet with a propane torch, broke two of his fingers, and beat him across the ribs until he stopped screaming and started making sounds he did not recognize as his own. What he remembered with excruciating clarity—the partial clarity that haunted him—was the moment one of his captors had leaned close and whispered that if he ever told anyone, they would find him and finish the job. What he could not remember at all was the final six hours before the police raid. That block of time was simply gone, a blank space in his mind that he could feel but could not enter. When he tried to explain what had happened to the FBI agent who debriefed him, he lost the thread mid-sentence, gestured helplessly, and stopped trying. He had never been able to put the event into words since. The words did not exist.

In the months after his rescue, Elias returned to his job as a park ranger, but the work felt unrecognizable. He had always loved the solitude of the backcountry, the quiet rhythm of checking trail markers and clearing downed branches. Now, every time a hiker approached from behind, his body reacted before his mind could catch up—his shoulders would lock, his breath would shorten, and he would find himself scanning the tree line for threats before he had consciously registered any sound. He began to avoid driving altogether, both as driver and passenger, because the sight of an unfamiliar vehicle pulling up behind him at a trailhead sent him into a state he could only describe as "white static." His supervisor accommodated him with desk duty, but the office brought its own terrors. When a routine equipment request took longer than expected, Elias was certain something bad was happening—that the delay meant someone was coming for him, that the system had been compromised. He checked the locks on the ranger station door four times before he could sit down at his desk, and he checked his apartment door and windows every night before bed, sometimes twice, sometimes three times, because he could not trust that he had done it correctly the first time.

Elias had come to believe that his body had been permanently damaged by what happened. Not just the physical scars—the crooked fingers, the nerve damage in his feet that made long hikes impossible—but something deeper. He felt that the structure of his flesh had been altered, that he was now a person who could be broken, and that this fact was visible to others. He avoided social contact almost entirely. When he did have to speak to someone—a coworker, a store clerk—he rehearsed the conversation in his head beforehand, cycling through possible questions and answers until he had a script, because the thought of being caught off guard by a question felt like being ambushed. He had stopped dating altogether. He could not imagine letting someone close enough to see the scars, to ask what happened, to expect him to explain something he could not explain. He was certain that he could not rely on other people; the men who had taken him had been strangers, but they had also been human, and that was enough to prove that trust was a calculation he could no longer make.

The emotional numbness came gradually, then all at once. He noticed it first when his mother called on his birthday and he felt nothing—not warmth, not irritation, just a flat, distant awareness that he should be feeling something. He began to numb his feelings deliberately, because the alternative was a terror so vast that it felt like it would swallow him whole. He had started to wonder if his reactions meant he was going crazy. The checking, the rehearsing, the way his body jumped at shadows—it did not feel like coping. It felt like coming apart.

What finally brought Elias to a therapist was a small thing. A hiker had thanked him for clearing a trail, and Elias had found himself unable to respond. His mouth had opened, then closed, then opened again. The hiker had looked at him with confusion, then concern, and had asked if he was okay. Elias had walked away without answering. That night, sitting alone in his apartment with all the lights on and the deadbolt turned, he realized that he was no longer living in the world. He was living in a small, locked room inside his head, and he did not know how to open the door. He was afraid that therapy would only confirm what he already suspected—that he was too far gone, that the damage was permanent. But he was also afraid of staying where he was. So he made an appointment, and he showed up, and he sat in the waiting room with his hands on his knees, rehearsing what he would say, knowing he would lose the thread, hoping that this time, someone would understand.
